# Mahāsāropama Sutta (MN 29 (PTS MN i 192))
**ID:** MN 29 (PTS MN i 192)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahāsāropama Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 192

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahāsāropama Sutta* ("The Longer Simile of the Heartwood") is the twenty-ninth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. The discourse was delivered by the Buddha at Mount Vulture Peak near Rājagaha shortly after Devadatta's departure and secession from the Sangha [Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli & Bhikkhu Bodhi 1995; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Hazra 1994]. Prompted by Devadatta's pursuit of personal fame, gain, and honor through supernormal attainments, the Buddha warns the mendicants against becoming complacent or intoxicated with intermediate spiritual gains [Bhikkhu Bodhi 2005; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Schober 1997; Wijayaratna 1990].
Using the simile of a seeker gathering timber who mistakes twigs and leaves, outer bark, inner bark, or sapwood for core wood, the Buddha illustrates how practitioners may settle for worldly gain and honor, moral discipline, concentration, or knowledge and vision (*ñāṇa-dassana*), exalting themselves and disparaging others [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Narasabho 1971; Pye 1978; Webster 2005]. The sutta stresses that none of these intermediate achievements constitutes the final purpose of the holy life; rather, the ultimate goal and true heartwood is unshakeable deliverance of mind (*akuppā cetovimutti*) [Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli & Bhikkhu Bodhi 1995; SuttaCentral].
In terms of parallels and text reuse, SuttaCentral records an extant parallel in Chinese translation at EĀ 43.4, confirmed by Buswell and Lopez as an untitled recension in the *Ekottarikāgama* [SuttaCentral; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. DharmaNexus detects cross-language alignments with Chinese Āgama texts (T 26 and T 125) as well as the Sanskrit *Saṅghabhedavastu* and the Sanskrit and Tibetan recensions of the *Śrāvakabhūmi* in the *Yogācārabhūmi* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali Canon, the text forms an intimate pair with the immediately following *Cūḷasāropama Sutta* (MN 30), with which it shares nearly identical content and extensive textual reuse comprising over 600 shared segments [DharmaNexus; Kingsbury 2002; Rogell 2003; SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus also records substantial internal reuse with the *Udumbarika Sutta* (DN 25), the *Cātuma Sutta* (MN 67), and several nipātas of the Aṅguttara and Saṁyutta Nikāyas [DharmaNexus].
